To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) risk perception to EHS risks is influenced by individual level characteristics, and (2) individual characteristics play different explanatory roles for different categories of EHS risk.

the individual level characteristics that most explain risk perceptions vary between risk categories and that the most influential individual level characteristics vary across the three risk categories examined in this research.
the influence of individual level characteristics like age, education, income, race, gender, and perceptual biases on risk perceptions to different categories of EHS hazards varies significantly.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how risk perception differences can be explained by the individual level characteristics of respondents and by the category of ESH risk appraised.
the development of a comprehensive framework for understanding the interplay between individual level characteristics and risk categories in explaining risk perceptions.

the individual and cumulative effects of various individual level factors on risk perception differences between categories of Ehs hazards and contributes to the literature by (1) providing empirical insights into how the individual level variables that have been found to influence risk perceptions in previous studies can be used to explain risk perceptions to different categories of EHS hazards, and (2) providing a new conceptual framework for understanding risk perceptions to various EHS risks that can be used to inform future research
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the individual level characteristics examined here can be used to predict risk perceptions to EHS risks in general but the explanatory power of these characteristics varies between categories of Ehs risks.
the individual and cumulative role that various individual level characteristics play in characterizing EHS risk perceptions varies across the categories of EHS hazards.
the interplay of the category of ESH hazard appraised and the prominent individual level variables that best explain observed differences is not uniform.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

risk perception differences between various categories of Ehs risks can be explained to a large extent according to the interrelation between the risk category appraised and the individual characteristics that are most relevant for the risk category in question.

the individual level characteristics that are most important to predict the public risk perceptions to various EHS risks are not only those that are most commonly studied in the literature (e.g., personal demographics and socio-economic factors), but also those that have not been examined before (e.g., media use and perceptual filters).
the individual level characteristics that explain risk perceptions to a particular EHS hazard are dependent on the category of risk being appraised.
The main takeaway from our work is that
risk perception researchers should be aware of the interplay between risk categories and individual level characteristics in their research designs.
the individual level variables that best explain risk perceptions to various types of EHS risks vary according to the category of E HS risk studied.

individual level characteristics may not have the same explanatory role for all categories of EHS hazards, and that risk perception differences across risk categories can be better explained by the interaction of individual characteristics and the type of risk appraised.
